endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Ochsner Health, for example, requested real-time nudges to improve HCC documentation for specific diagnoses at the point of care after they noticed initial risk profile degradation for visits utilizing ambient scribe.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether real-time point-of-care nudges built on ambient scribe outputs and EHR data close documentation gaps. The only support is one guidance report describing a single health system's request for such nudges after it observed risk profile degradation in scribe-assisted visits.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies measuring the hazard. The single endorsing source describes one system's request, which is an observation rather than an evaluation. Under GRADE conventions, no certainty rating can be assigned because no comparison of nudged and unnudged documentation exists.

The guidance reports that Ochsner Health asked its vendor for real-time nudges on HCC documentation after noticing risk profile degradation in visits using the ambient scribe. The report does not state whether the nudges were built, what they cost, how often they fired, or whether risk scores recovered, so adopters cannot yet estimate return or clinician burden.

commentary.research_gap: Health systems need controlled or stepped-wedge evaluations that compare scribe-assisted visits with and without point-of-care nudges, measuring diagnosis capture, coding accuracy, false-positive prompt rates, clinician time and alert fatigue, and whether added diagnoses are clinically supported rather than driven by payment incentives. Studies should first quantify how often ambient scribe notes omit diagnoses relative to clinician-authored notes.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether scribe omissions or nudge performance differ for patients with non-English or interpreter-mediated visits remains unknown, and systems serving these patients should not assume the Ochsner experience applies to them.
